review_comments: I am a bit confused about the relationship between create rented and createlocked and convert to alloc. Why does `CreateLocked` mean `convertToAlloc` is false? It looks like, in most cases, `CreateRented` would also have `convertToAlloc` be false.

Scenarios:
1) `isLocked`=true + `convertToAlloc`=false. When called by pre-existing "Clone()" path (the buffer is known already).
2) `isLocked`=false+ `convertToAlloc`=false. Basically the pre-existing path with the exception of the "Clone()" path.
3) `isLocked`=true + `convertToAlloc`=false. New fast path for primitives (not arrays and objects). The size is known from the provided JSON length and the provided buffer is not pooled.
4) `isLocked`=false+ `convertToAlloc`=true. New fast path for arrays and objects. The size is not yet known, so we want to use a pooled buffer until we know the final size, and then release the pooled buffer after creating a non-pooled alloc.

Thanks for the clarification. I will come back and re-read the combination to understand it better.

Maybe parts of this explanation should be added to comments in source.
I added a table in comments to doc the behavior
Was this used?
Nope, although Intellisense falsely reported it was. There's anothor ctor with just the length that is called from one location.
Why did we remove this `Debug.Assert`? Add it back.

The Assert was moved into the `Enlarge()` that this method  (`Append`) calls.

The serializer fast-path calls into this method to append, but will never pass the `if` check just after this and call into `Enlarge`.
Any harm it keeping it here too? If not, we should keep it to be clear about the expected invariant, in case the code evolves.

The first line in `Enlarge()` does the Assert, and `Enlarge()` is only called from this one location. I don't see value in duplicating the Assert or moving it up.

However, perhaps removing `Enlarge()` is better.

> The first line in `Enlarge()` does the Assert, and `Enlarge()` is only called from this one location. I don't see value in duplicating the Assert or moving it up.

I see. Removing the extra debug.assert makes sense. Thanks for the explanation.

> However, perhaps removing `Enlarge()` is better.

inlining issue?
I don't think it is an inlining issue since no automatic inlining is done when there is any condition AFAIK. However, I added back the Enlarge anyway.
The double space after a period appears to be a pattern in this code base -- @bartonjs?

I'm old, so I initially learned to type on a typewriter, and double-space-after-period is built into my hands. (And, personally, I think generally looks better in fixed with fonts, which is why the concept was introduced in the first place).

I'd leave it as is, since it's just an indentation/move that has no other formatting change to it (whether it matched or didn't match the style).  If you want my style opinion, clearly it's double-space-after-period.  But if you're merely asking if it'll make me annoyed if it gets changed: nah :smile:.
I don't plan on changing. Thanks. If someone wants to make the spacing consistent (and any other things) then yes that's fine but should be in a separate PR.

So, looks like this change alone is what is giving us the perf win during serialization. Is that correct?

> Avoids dictionary lookup during serialization for every element of a collection (if elements are all the same type).

Does this optimization only apply to elements of collections or can it apply to all properties on classes (that are not polymorphic)?

> Does this optimization only apply to elements of collections or can it apply to all properties on classes (that are not polymorphic)?

> ~1.1x faster for objects (for a sample POCO).

Looks like you already answered this question with your benchmark result in the PR description and it is: Yes it applies to properties of POCOs too.
How's test coverage for all these changes? Are we still at 100% for JsonElement/JsonDocument?

```suggestion
            bool useArrayPools = true)
```

Make optional so existing calls don't need to change?
Since this is internal code, I prefer the explicit parameter for understandability.
What does `_isLocked` mean, now? Maybe we should rename it since its use, the comment, and name no longer match.
It means basically the same as it did before -- the array is the correct size and thus shouldn't be increased in size.

Are we allowed to just assign the static right up front (and then simplify `CreateForLiteral`), or is there some value in doing it only at runtime (with a null check, below) on the first call to Parse.
```C#
private static JsonDocument s_nullLiteral = Create(JsonConstants.FalseValue.ToArray());
```

We could, but it would increase startup perf for the standard (non serializer) code path. Also, the "null" literal isn't actually even used by the serializer, only when the new API is called manually.
The explicit `propertyName` isn't used anymore, so was removed.

Would it be beneficial (or even possible) to move this check into the caller (looks like there is only one callsite), here?
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/746ca52cf3405d9faeb3d2644b56e3761b375002/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonConverterOfT.cs#L337

Also, please add a comment explaining what this check is doing and when it will be false such that we can skip calling `options.GetOrAddClass` (something inspired by your PR description would be a good starting point).

Isn't this check already covered by the `type != TypeToConvert` condition here:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/746ca52cf3405d9faeb3d2644b56e3761b375002/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonConverterOfT.cs#L333-L343
> Would it be beneficial (or even possible) to move this check into the caller (looks like there is only one callsite), here?

It is possible, but I think it breaks some encapsulation by that method. Also, the `PolymorphicJsonPropertyInfo` field should be changed from public to private since it already exposed by `GetPolymorphicJsonPropertyInfo()` which should normally be used to obtain that.

> Also, please add a comment..

Yep. Will do
How large can `size` be here, in the worst case, and how come we can get away with using GC-backed array here? `JsonDocument` APIs are meant to be amortized non-allocating for payloads under 2 MB.

Much of the optimizations in this PR are due to not using the pooled buffer, since it was previously created and then converted to a normal alloc in "Clone()" and in all cases, except object and array, using the pooled buffer was not helpful for perf.

`size` can be the size of the largest JSON value (utf8Json.Length).

> `size` can be the size of the largest JSON value (utf8Json.Length).

And does this **only** happen in similar code paths where previously `Clone()` would be called?

**To confirm:** Are we still non-allocating for the standard use of JsonDocument/JsonElement parse, random-access, and dispose, or does this code path come into play in that usage in some way?

> Are we still non-allocating for the standard use of JsonDocument/JsonElement parse, random-access, and dispose, or does this code path come into play in that usage in some way?

Yes; the intent was to use the pooled memory exactly the same for the standard usage. Also I just verified that the "before" and "after" results have the same values for the "Allocated" column.
Is it possible/worth it to avoid the temporary ArrayPool rent to begin with?

Since it can grow based on length, using the temp pool has advantages since it prevents allocs in those cases. When creating the "real" (non-pooled) buffer, it is created with the correct (trimmed) size which also prevents an alloc if we wanted to trim the size.

However, it is possible to add a mode that we try to detect whether small JSON will fit into a default buffer size, and not trim it afterwards. For example, if we know we are deserializing a number or string and not an object or array.
I update the PR to address this as well as other improvements including caching of literal values.
